opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it was really about seeing how RL gets done at scale, in practice. When I was a student, I worked on Tianshou, the RL library, and in that world you're mostly running experiments on a single machine or a few GPUs, reproducing papers, trying to make the algorithms clean and fast. That taught me a lot about the details, but there's always a question in the back of your mind: what does this look like when it actually matters, when you're training something really big and the result has to work?

OpenAI was one of the few places where RL wasn't just a benchmark exercise. They had done Dota and the robotic hand work, and then RLHF was becoming central to how language models were trained. So the appeal was that the research and the engineering were really tied together. You couldn't separate "having a good idea" from "building infrastructure that lets the idea run reliably on thousands of GPUs." I'm someone who enjoys the infrastructure side a lot, so that combination felt natural to me.

The other part was the people. You could sit next to someone who had actually debugged these systems for years, and you learn things you'd never find in a paper: which tricks really matter, which ones are noise, how you know an experiment is going wrong before the curves tell you. That tacit knowledge is hard to get anywhere else, and I felt the fastest way to learn how RL research is really done was to be in the room where it was happening at that scale.

r001.rationale: Weng contrasts student work on a single machine or a few GPUs, focused on reproducing papers, with learning how RL research is done at OpenAI’s scale, including its practical methods and tacit knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For me the appeal was pretty simple: I wanted to see how the people who actually built the field did the work, not just read about it. Before OpenAI, a lot of what I knew about reinforcement learning came from papers and from building open-source tools like Tianshou, where you reproduce algorithms, debug them, and try to make them run fast and reliably. That teaches you a lot about the mechanics, but it doesn't really show you how research questions get chosen or how a team decides what's worth months of compute and effort.

OpenAI was one of the few places where reinforcement learning wasn't a side project. It was central to things like Dota, robotics, and later RLHF for language models. So the people there had lived through the problems where RL breaks at scale, the reward hacking, the instability, the infrastructure headaches, and they had opinions grounded in actual experience rather than theory. Being around that, you absorb taste: what experiments are worth running, what results you should distrust, when to stop tuning and change the approach instead.

The other piece was the engineering culture. A lot of RL research is really systems work, like keeping thousands of environments running, moving data efficiently, making training reproducible. I care a lot about that side, and OpenAI treated infrastructure as a first-class part of research rather than something you hand off. That combination of strong research intuition and serious engineering was exactly what I wanted to learn from.

r001.rationale: The response says papers and open-source work taught mechanics but not how research questions are chosen or prioritized. It does not mention an ad hoc approach or associate one with small academic groups.

astra-6.text: What appealed to me was the chance to learn by doing, alongside people with a lot of experience in reinforcement learning. I wanted to understand more than the methods themselves—I wanted to see how researchers choose a problem, design experiments, and make sense of results when things don’t work as expected. OpenAI seemed like a place where I could get that kind of hands-on exposure and develop my own research judgment.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning research methods and workflows at OpenAI, but does not mention moving beyond an ad hoc approach or associate that approach with small academic groups.

sol-6.1.text: What appealed to me was the chance to learn from people with a lot of experience in reinforcement learning and see how they approached research day to day. I wanted to understand the whole process—how you choose a question, design experiments, and make sense of results when they don’t match your expectations. OpenAI seemed like a place where I could learn that by working alongside people.
